extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, litigators, judges, and advanced law students interested in patent validity doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: A doctrinal and procedural analysis of how the law-fact distinction is applied across major patent-validity requirements (written description, enablement, utility, eligibility, novelty, and nonobviousness), and the consequences for trial practice and appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention; the inquiry “depends on the nature of the invention and the amount of knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art by the disclosure.” The core question: does the specification convey clearly to those skilled in the art that the inventor invented the specific claimed subject matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written-description analysis requires comparing the original application or specification to the issued claim(s) from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art. It may be informed by expert testimony and resembles claim construction. Model jury instructions ask whether a person of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the subject matter claimed; the requirement “may be satisfied by any combination of the words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, etc.” Practical note: written description is often decided by juries (frequently via general verdicts), which complicates appellate review because of deferential standards applied to jury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent’s specification must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is determined by reading the patent from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill and often relies on factual findings (e.g., need for undue experimentation). The Federal Circuit characterizes enablement as a question of law based on underlying factual findings; in jury trials the factual underpinnings are reviewed for substantial evidence or clear error. Enablement decisions often appear as mixed law-fact issues and are frequently submitted to juries via general verdicts, affecting appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. § 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be useful; § 101 requires that the inventor discovered something 'new and useful.' In many cases demonstrating utility is straightforward, but in life and chemical sciences utility is significant (e.g., a laboratory promise does not establish utility for human treatment claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts almost always identify utility as a question of fact, typically relying on expert testimony or skilled artisan evidence. Historical citations trace factual treatment of utility to policy considerations about evaluating case-specific scientific testimony. The factual framing influences whether juries decide utility and how appellate courts review those decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility (§ 101) as a legal question with factual exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility is generally treated as a question of law (e.g., whether claim is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter and meets judicial exceptions), but it can be treated as factual when the dispute centers on whether the patent involves well-understood, routine, or conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit often treats eligibility as legal, yet makes exceptions where factual showings (e.g., well-understood, routine, conventional) determine eligibility; this creates inconsistent practice and strategic uncertainty for litigants about whether eligibility will be decided by judge or jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty ensures the claimed invention is different from prior technology; a claim must be distinct from prior art under § 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not the primary focus of this chunk, novelty is referenced as a primarily fact-intensive inquiry about what prior art discloses and how the claim differs. Like other validity doctrines, its characterization as law or fact affects whether a judge or jury decides it and how appellate courts review findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) — ultimate legal conclusion with factual underpinnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonobviousness is ultimately a question of law, but it 'lends itself to several basic factual inquiries' per Graham: determining the scope and content of the prior art, ascertaining differences between prior art and the claims, resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art, and considering secondary considerations (objective indicia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Supreme Court in Graham and KSR frames obviousness as a legal determination built on specific factual findings, in practice courts (and juries) often decide obviousness via general verdicts and appellate review can be deferential. KSR rejected a rigid TSM test and urged courts to consider inferences and creativity of a POSITA, and emphasized that courts should make the analysis explicit; nevertheless, lower courts and the Federal Circuit have continued to apply fact-driven bright-line tests (e.g., TSM, analogous art, motivation to combine) that push obviousness toward jury resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham framework / factual Graham factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries required by Graham: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) consideration of secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are treated as findings of fact that inform the legal determination of obviousness. Courts and model jury instructions may submit these factual questions to juries (preferably via special interrogatories) so that the judge can make an explicit legal ruling applying those facts; failure to obtain explicit findings (i.e., a black-box general verdict) impedes reasoned appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching–suggestion–motivation (TSM) test / motivation to combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A requirement historically adopted by the Federal Circuit that a patent challenger identify a specific 'teaching[,] suggestion[,] or motivation' to combine prior art references to support an obviousness challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TSM test was treated as a question of fact by the Federal Circuit and led to many cases going to trial because proof of a motivation to combine required factfinding. The Supreme Court in KSR criticized the Federal Circuit’s rigid application of TSM, favoring a more flexible approach that accounts for inferences and creativity from a POSITA; despite KSR, the Federal Circuit has continued to apply TSM-like motivation/analogous-art requirements in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for relevance of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: For a prior art reference to be relevant to an obviousness inquiry, it must be from an analogous art—that is, sufficiently related to the problem addressed by the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit treats analogous art as a question of fact. Determinations about whether a reference is analogous (and thus relevant) affect whether the reference can be used in an obviousness combination and often require factfinding amenable to jury resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction / interpretation of patent instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge determines the scope of the patent by construing its claims in light of the specification, prosecution history, and sometimes extrinsic evidence, from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art; construction of written instruments is a judicial function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Markman) treats claim construction as ultimately a question of law for the judge, even when factual inquiries are necessary. The Court emphasized that judges are trained in exegesis and are 'likely to do better than jurors' at construing written instruments. Claim construction informs other validity and infringement analyses and is reviewed de novo (subject to the Teva decision clarifying review of subsidiary facts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review (de novo vs. deferential / clear-error / substantial-evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether appellate courts review a validity determination de novo (law) or deferentially (factual findings reviewed for clear error or substantial evidence) depends on whether the underlying issue is characterized as legal or factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit practice is inconsistent: some doctrines are described as legal questions reviewed de novo, others as factual. Where juries render general verdicts, appellate courts often apply deferential review to the underlying factual findings, which can yield practical deference to jury determinations even for issues the Supreme Court describes as legal. This inconsistency creates strategic uncertainty for litigants and complicates appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many validity inquiries (written description, enablement, obviousness, claim construction to some extent) are conducted from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the relevant art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations about how a POSITA would understand disclosures, whether the POSITA could practice the invention without undue experimentation, or what a POSITA would find obvious are often informed by expert testimony and are central factual inputs that shape the legal conclusions. Jury instructions commonly ask jurors to assess issues from this viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective indicia of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others that can be used as objective indicia to show nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations are part of the Graham framework and are factual inquiries that can counterbalance evidence suggesting obviousness. Courts should explicitly consider and make findings on these factors; presenting them to a jury via special interrogatories can preserve appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special interrogatories / advisory jury and written findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural practice recommending that when juries decide complex validity issues (e.g., obviousness), courts should use special interrogatories tied to Graham factors or obtain advisory verdicts so that the jury’s underlying factual findings are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Case Management Judicial Guide and some district model instructions prefer special interrogatories to reveal the jury's factual findings (scope/content of prior art, level of skill, motivation to combine, secondary considerations). With explicit factual answers, judges and appellate courts can apply appropriate mixed standards (deferential to facts, de novo to legal conclusions) and produce reasoned written orders. Avoiding black-box general verdicts is emphasized as a best practice to enable meaningful review.
